title: Serving Runtime: Architecture, Scheduling, Profiling & Ops Playbook
author: Asha Patel
content:
Overview

This document consolidates the serving runtime architecture, kernel scheduling and heuristics, profiling playbooks, benchmarking suite guidance, recent release notes, known issues, and the primary runtime runbooks used by the serving team. It is intended as a team wiki / reference for engineers and on-call responders who operate Redwood's inference runtime.

Scope

- Audience: serving runtime engineers, SREs, performance engineers, and solutions engineers performing private deployments.
- Includes: architecture diagrams (textual), kernel and scheduling policies, profiling steps, benchmarking scenarios and scripts, release summary for the last published runtime, known issues with mitigations, and incident runbooks.

Runtime Architecture (high level)

The runtime is composed of the following logical components. The text below mirrors the topology deployed in Hosted, Dedicated, and Private.

1) Front Door / API Gateway
- Responsibilities: authentication, rate-limiting, request shaping, and early validation.
- Owned by: edge-team; interface contract: JSON payload with model_id, input, call_options.

2) Smart Router
- Responsibilities: routing requests to appropriate pool (latency-tier, cost-tier, region), model variant selection, fallback policy.
- Policies: latency-first (p99), cost-first (budget-aware), region-affinity.

3) Scheduler (kernel scheduling & batching)
- Responsibilities: continuous & transactional batching, kernel selection for execution, preemption for high-priority requests, slot allocation on GPU instances.
- Key primitives: batch window, max_batch_size, evictable_slot, preemption_class.

4) Executor / Kernel Manager
- Responsibilities: select quantized vs. fp16 kernels, sequence-length tuning, memory-aware kernel choice, kernel warmup.

5) KV Cache Service
- Responsibilities: prefix caching, inter-request KV reuse, eviction based on LRU with TTL per model.

6) Metrics & Tracing
- Responsibilities: per-token latency, kernel busy %, batch utilization, memory headroom, and tail-latency histograms.

SLOs and Thresholds (production targets)

- Per-request p95 latency: <= 120 ms for latency-tier small models (< 1B tokens/session).
- Per-token p99 latency: <= 250 ms for interactive workloads.
- Throughput utilization target: 60-80% GPU utilization under steady-state.
- Error budget: 99.9% availability per month for Hosted routes.

Kernel Scheduling: Design and Heuristics

Goals: minimize end-to-end latency while achieving high GPU throughput and predictable tail behavior.

Key algorithms and modes:

- Continuous Batching (default): requests are pooled into a moving window (batch_window_ms, default 8 ms) and dispatched when either batch_window_ms expires or max_batch_size reached. This mode favors throughput with low added latency.

- Priority-aware Scheduling: requests annotated with priority: realtime, interactive, background. Realtime preempts background batches by reserving evictable slots.

- Sequence-length-aware Kernel Selection: short sequences prefer kernels optimized for small seq len (lower launch overhead). Long sequences use kernels with fused-matrix attention.

- Memory-aware Placement: scheduler consults executor for per-kernel estimated scratch memory. If memory headroom < threshold, scheduler reduces batch sizes or routes to dedicated lower-concurrency nodes.

Config table (common config keys)

| key | description | recommended default | notes |
|-----|-------------|---------------------|-------|
| batch_window_ms | max wait before dispatch | 8 | tuning knob for latency vs throughput |
| max_batch_size | hard cap on batch size | 64 | depends on model and GPU (A100/RTX) |
| preemption_class | priority threshold for preemption | realtime | values: realtime/interactive/background |
| kernel_selection_policy | ordered list of kernels to try | [quantized, fp16, fp32] | fallback order |
| mem_headroom_threshold_mb | required free mem to accept batch | 512 | reduce when under memory pressure |

Profiling Playbook (how to profile a slowdown)

When performance regresses, follow these steps:

1) Reproduce in isolation
- Use bench-runner to replay representative traffic with prod-like config.
- Command: ./bench-runner --scenario interactive --model <model> --rps 50 --duration 300s

2) Collect top-level metrics
- Grafana dashboards: "Runtime / Host / Kernel" and "Runtime / Routing / Batching".
- Key metrics: kernel_busy_pct, batch_size_histogram, avg_wait_ms, kv_cache_hit_rate, gpu_mem_headroom_mb.

3) Enable tracing for sample requests
- Toggle sampled tracing: curl -X POST "${APIGW}/v1/debug/tracing?sample_rate=0.05"
- Capture trace: use jaeger UI and look for long waiting spans in scheduler and executor.

4) Run micro-profiling on node
- SSH into node (or use internal profiling agent): sudo /opt/redwood/bin/profile-runtime.sh --duration 60 --out /tmp/profile.tar.gz
- Tools collected: perf, nvprof/nvtx, python-trace, allocator stats.

5) Kernel-level profiling
- Use kernel-debugger utility to capture kernel launch times and occupancy: /opt/redwood/bin/kernel-debugger --model <id> --profile-kernels --out kernels.csv
- Look for high kernel-launch overhead or low occupancy on long-seq kernels.

6) Triage and mitigate
- If batch_wait dominates: reduce batch_window_ms or route high-priority traffic to low-latency pool.
- If kernel_launch dominates: enable kernel warmup or switch to an alternate kernel variant.
- If memory pressure: reduce max_batch_size or increase node memory on fleet.

Benchmarking Suite (how we measure performance and regressions)

The benchmarking suite is the canonical harness used for release validation and regression tests. It lives under infra/benchmarks and is executed by CI and manual runs.

Canonical scenarios:
- interactive-short: 8 ms arrival jitter, sequence lengths 8-64, 1-10 RPS per instance.
- completion-long: bursty arrivals, outputs up to 2048 tokens, rps < 1.
- batching-throughput: sustained high-rps to exercise batching kernel throughput.

Standard metrics captured:
- tokens/sec, p50/p95/p99 latency (request and token-level), batch_size distribution, GPU utilization, cost-per-1M-tokens (estimate).

Running the suite locally (example)
1) Checkout repo: git clone git@repo:redwood/benchmarks.git
2) Build runner: make -C benchmarks build
3) Run: ./benchmarks/run_bench.py --scenario interactive-short --model-id rdm-7b-quant --instances 4 --duration 600 --out ./results/interactive-7b.json

Release Notes (latest runtime release)

Version: runtime v3.2.1 (released 2029-11-20)
- Feature: added adaptive batch-window tuning (auto-adjusts batch_window_ms per route based on p95 latency target).
- Feature: kernel warmup improvements for quantized kernels (reduces first-call latency by ~40%).
- Fix: corrected memory leak in KV cache when using multi-tenant prefixes.
- Fix: scheduler hot-loop that caused elevated CPU on high-rps workloads.
- Known limitation: adaptive tuning currently disabled for Private on-prem single-node installs due to telemetry requirement.

Known Issues & Workarounds

1) Symptom: p99 latency spikes at low RPS with long sequences.
- Root cause: scheduler builds larger batches waiting for max_batch_size before dispatch on long-seq workloads.
- Workaround: set batch_window_ms=2 for the route or enable "always-short-window" tuning profile.

2) Symptom: OOM kills on mixed workloads (some long-seq, some short-seq).
- Root cause: naive kernel memory estimates for fused attention.
- Workaround: set mem_headroom_threshold_mb to 1024 and route long-seq workloads to dedicated pool.

3) Symptom: high kernel_launch latency observed on first requests after deploy.
- Workaround: add kernel warmup step in rollout (see "Rollout checklist" below).

Runtime Runbooks (operational procedures)

Incident: Elevated p99 token latency
1) Pager triggers: p99_token_latency > 300 ms for 10 minutes.
2) Initial actions (0-5 min):
  a) Acknowledge incident in PagerDuty.
  b) Check Grafana top-level: kernel_busy_pct, avg_wait_ms, batch_size_histogram.
  c) Identify affected routes and models.
3) Escalation (5-15 min):
  a) If avg_wait_ms > 50ms: reduce batch_window_ms for affected routes or enable route-level low-latency pool.
  b) If kernel_busy_pct > 95% and GPU utilization saturating: enable autoscale burst (if capacity available) or shift lower-priority traffic to background queue.
4) Recovery (15-60 min):
  a) If workaround applied and metrics return to normal, document corrective action and run a postmortem.

Rollout checklist (for runtime / kernel changes)
1) Run full benchmark suite and collect baseline.
2) Deploy to canary pool (1-5% traffic).
3) Run 30-minute smoke bench against canary.
4) Monitor: p50/p95/p99, error-rate, kernel_launch_latency, mem_headroom_mb.
5) If stable, roll to wider pool with staged increases (5%, 25%, 100%).
6) Ensure warmup job runs on new nodes before receiving production traffic: /opt/redwood/bin/warmup-kernels --models <list>.

Team Wiki & Ownership

- Primary owner: serving-runtime team (owner: Asha Patel).
- Secondary owners: eng-sre, infra-performance.
- On-call rotation: serving-runtime 1-week rotation; contact via #oncall-serving-runtime slack.
- Links: internal perf repo (git@repo:redwood/serving-runtime-perf.git), CI jobs (Jenkins/bench-runtime), infra dashboards (Grafana link).

Appendix: Useful Commands and Snippets

- Run single-node profiler:
  sudo /opt/redwood/bin/profile-runtime.sh --duration 60 --out /tmp/profile.tar.gz

- Run bench-runner (example):
  ./bench-runner --scenario interactive --model rdm-7b-quant --rps 50 --duration 300

- Switch route to low-latency pool:
  curl -X POST "${ADMIN_API}/routes/<route_id>/override" -H 'Authorization: Bearer <token>' -d '{"pool": "low-latency"}'

- Warmup kernels during rollout:
  /opt/redwood/bin/warmup-kernels --models rdm-7b-quant,rdm-1b-fp16

Document maintenance

- Owner is responsible for updating the release notes and runbooks at each runtime release. Add reviewers when making changes to kernel heuristics.

If you find gaps in this playbook or new recurring issues, add an entry here and notify reviewers for triage.
